name: Wounded Warrior Project: mental health (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: Wounded Warrior Project's mental health programmes for US veterans.
summary: Wounded Warrior Project pays four academic medical centres (Warrior Care Network) to run two- and three-week intensive PTSD programmes and outpatient therapy for post-9/11 veterans, and runs its own counselling, Project Odyssey retreats, WWP Talk calls and case coordination. Our model of its mental health spending in fiscal 2025 ($98.7M; 1,286 veterans in the intensive programmes, about 12,000 others) takes the effect from trials of trauma-focused therapy in military personnel (about 0.85 SD on depression measures at the end of treatment, fading over about four years) and adds the suicides it averts; it comes to about {{result}} years of healthy life per $1,000, low because each person costs about $11,000 and a WELLBY is worth a fifteenth of a healthy year at the site's rate. The therapy and support branches are discounted for missing data (no controlled evaluation of WWP's outpatient therapy, counselling, Project Odyssey or WWP Talk); the intensive programmes are measured. The biggest uncertainties are how long the effect lasts and how much of it the VA's own PTSD care would have given anyway.

rows.label: Effect of trauma-focused CBT on PTSD symptoms in military personnel and veterans, against waitlist or usual care (SD)

source.title: Kitchiner, Lewis, Roberts and Bisson (2019), Active duty and ex-serving military personnel with post-traumatic stress disorder treated with psychological therapies: systematic review and meta-analysis, European Journal of Psychotraumatology 10(1):1684226
source.quote: CBT with a trauma focus (CBT-TF) was associated with the largest evidence of effect when compared to waitlist/usual care in reducing PTSD symptoms post treatment (10 studies; n = 524; SMD -1.22, -1.78 to -0.66).

rows.explainer: The effect for the intensive programmes: a Cochrane-method review of 24 trials in active-duty and ex-serving personnel, of the treatments Warrior Care Network delivers (CPT, Prolonged Exposure), at the end of treatment. Range the 95% CI (interval 0.95). Its ten trials include the one controlled trial of the two-week massed format (Foa et al. 2018, JAMA 319:354: 10 sessions of Prolonged Exposure in two weeks for 370 soldiers, 3.70 PSS-I points better than minimal contact, 95% CI 0.72 to 6.68, about 0.58 baseline SDs), which is not blended in again; that it sits below the pool is part of iop_evidence_adj. Warrior Care Network has no controlled trial of its own; its programme data (Held et al. 2021, 452 veterans at Rush: PCL-5 falling about 22 points from about 56, roughly 1.8 baseline SDs, no control group) are a check, above the trials' controlled effect as uncontrolled change is.

rows.label: Effect on depression as a share of the effect on PTSD symptoms

source.title: Held et al. (2024), Veterans' 12-month PTSD and depression outcomes following 2- and 3-week intensive cognitive processing therapy-based treatment, European Journal of Psychotraumatology 15(1)
source.quote: Participants across both ITPs reported large PTSD (d = 0.98) and moderate to large depression symptom reductions (d = 0.69) from baseline to 12-month follow-up.

rows.explainer: The site's WELLBYs per SD-year are measured on wellbeing and depression scales, so the PTSD effect is put on the depression scale first. Anchor: in Warrior Care Network's own 12-month follow-up of 1,134 veterans after Rush's two- and three-week programmes, PTSD fell by d = 0.98 and depression by d = 0.69 (Held et al. 2024, European Journal of Psychotraumatology, PMC11110869: 'large PTSD (d = 0.98) and moderate to large depression symptom reductions (d = 0.69)'), a ratio of 0.70. 0.7 (0.5-0.9).

rows.label: Initial effect on depression and wellbeing measures (SD)
rows.explainer: The trials' PTSD effect on the depression scale: about 0.85 SD at the end of treatment, before the adjustments (evidence, counterfactual, completion).

rows.label: Years until the effect has faded to nothing (linear fade)

source.title: Held et al. (2024), European Journal of Psychotraumatology
source.quote: Effect sizes for change in PCL-5 (d = 1.26) and PHQ-9 (d = 0.91) reflected large improvements from baseline to post-treatment, and moderate to large improvements from baseline to 12-month follow-up (d = 0.98 and d = 0.69, respectively)

rows.explainer: Warrior Care Network's veterans kept 78% of the PTSD gain and 76% of the depression gain a year on (d 1.26 to 0.98, and 0.91 to 0.69). A straight fade keeping 76% of the depression gain at a year (the scale the WELLBYs use) reaches zero at 1 / (1 - 0.76) = 4.2 years (4.5 on the PTSD scale). Range: 2 years if the 29% who answered at 12 months were the ones who did well (the authors call low follow-up completion a limitation) to 8 if the gains plateau, as longer follow-ups of CPT suggest.

rows.label: Fade of the effect per year (SD)
rows.explainer: Context: the linear fade implied.

rows.label: Continuous discount rate
rows.explainer: The shared discount rate, continuously compounded.

rows.label: Discount factor for the fading effect
rows.formula: if(continuous_discount_rate > 0, (continuous_discount_rate * effect_duration_years - 1 + exp(-(continuous_discount_rate * effect_duration_years))) / (0.5 * (continuous_discount_rate * effect_duration_years) * (continuous_discount_rate * effect_duration_years)), 1)
rows.explainer: Present value of the triangle (linear fade to zero) at the shared rate, as a share of its undiscounted area; as in the HLI models.

rows.label: SD-years per person treated, discounted
WELLBYs per veteran in the intensive programmes
rows.explainer: SD-years at the site's one rate (@wellby_factors.wellbys_per_sd_year).

rows.label: People per household
rows.explainer: The site's US figure ({{row:household_size}} per consumer unit).

rows.label: Household multiplier (recipient plus spillovers)
rows.explainer: Each other household member gains the site's one share of the recipient's effect (HLI's, @wellby_factors). The 565 family members treated directly are counted as people reached as well; their own households' spillovers are small and left in.

rows.label: Effect of the centres' weekly outpatient therapy, as a share of the intensive programmes'
rows.explainer: What each outpatient got isn't reported (the 990 says only 'traditional outpatient therapy'): at these specialist centres much of it is weekly CPT or PE, the format of the trials behind the prior, but outside trials many patients stop early or never start the trauma-focused part. In a systematic review of 26 studies 28% of patients in outpatient mental health settings began trauma-centred CBT, and initiation was higher where staff had more exposure to the therapy (odds ratio 2.3) (van den Berk Clark et al. 2019, Psychiatric Services 70(8):703-713), against 90% completing the intensive programmes; those who stop keep part of the gain. This row is the whole delivery gap for the branch (implementation_adj is not applied again), and the branch stays thin. 0.6 (0.35-0.9).

source.title: van den Berk Clark et al. (2019), Factors associated with receipt of cognitive-behavioral therapy or prolonged exposure therapy among individuals with PTSD, Psychiatric Services 70(8):703-713
source.quote: The average weighted initiation rate was 6% in larger hospital systems with a high rate of trauma and 28% in outpatient mental health settings

rows.label: Effect of the centres' treatment and psychoeducation for family members, as a share of the intensive programmes'
rows.explainer: Our judgment, with no published effect for this group found: family members get treatment and psychoeducation, not a veteran's PTSD course, so a smaller effect, about a third of the veterans' therapy effect. 0.3 (0.1-0.6).

rows.label: Effect of WWP-paid counselling, as a share of the intensive programmes'
rows.explainer: About six sessions of general counselling from community providers, not necessarily trauma-focused. Anchor: in Kitchiner et al. 2019's direct comparison, present-centred (non-trauma-focused) therapy did about 0.5 SD less than trauma-focused CBT, leaving it roughly 0.6 of the effect; a shorter course than the trials' gives less again. 0.45 (0.25-0.7).

rows.label: WELLBYs per person in the centres' outpatient therapy
WELLBYs per person counselled
Initial effect of Project Odyssey, WWP Talk and case coordination on depression and wellbeing measures (SD)
rows.explainer: No controlled evaluation of these programmes exists (WWP reports satisfaction and goals met). Built from the research on such work: peer and lay support for depression gives small to moderate effects against usual care (Pfeiffer et al. 2011, General Hospital Psychiatry 33:29, SMD 0.59 in small trials; much smaller in larger ones), and outdoor and adventure programmes for veterans have only uncontrolled pre-post studies (Armitage et al. 2026, BMJ Open scoping review: 'evidence was heterogeneous and variable in outcome measurement'). 0.15 SD (0.03-0.4) for a five-day retreat with follow-up or five calls with a listener; coordination's effect is getting people into VA care, valued the same way.

rows.label: Years until the support branch's effect has faded to nothing
rows.explainer: A light-touch programme: the effect lasts months, not years. 0.75 years (3 months to 2 years), anchored on follow-ups of brief and peer interventions, which rarely show effects beyond a year.

rows.label: Discounting term for the support branch's fade
Discount factor for the support branch's fading effect
rows.explainer: The same triangle discount as above, over the support branch's shorter fade.

rows.label: WELLBYs per person in the support branch
Evidence adjustment, intensive programmes
rows.explainer: Trust in the trials' effect for these programmes. The one large trial of the two-week massed format (Foa et al. 2018, inside the pool) found about half the pooled effect (0.58 SD, SE 0.24, against the pool's 1.22); weighting it by precision against the rest of the pool (about 1.31 SD, SE 0.31) gives 0.70 of the pooled figure, and the rest of the pool's small trials and likely publication bias take a further 0.85: 0.70 × 0.85 = 0.60 (0.45-0.9), within HLI's psychotherapy discounts (0.5-0.7). The conversion of a depression-scale effect into life satisfaction is the site's (@wellby_factors.wellbys_per_sd_year), not adjusted again here; the gap between a waitlist and the veterans' real alternative is in the counterfactual.

rows.label: Share of the effect that wouldn't have happened anyway, intensive programmes
rows.explainer: The trials' effect is against waitlist or usual care, so care as usual is already netted out. Below 1 for treatment these veterans would have got and the trials' controls didn't: the VA offers CPT and PE free to every enrolled veteran, but only a minority with PTSD start them and fewer finish a full course (most VA PTSD patients get fewer than eight sessions). Veterans who seek out a two-week programme are more motivated than most and some would have finished therapy elsewhere. 0.7 (0.5-0.9).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, therapy branch
rows.explainer: As the intensive programmes (0.60), with the dose differences in opt_dose_vs_iop, opt_family_dose_vs_iop and cns_dose_vs_iop.

rows.label: Share of the effect that wouldn't have happened anyway, therapy branch
rows.explainer: Weekly outpatient therapy and counselling are what the VA, TRICARE and community care offer too, so more of it would have happened anyway than for the intensive programmes: 0.6 (0.35-0.85).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, support branch
rows.explainer: The effect above is already a judgment from the literature on light-touch support, set low; this adjusts only for self-selection of satisfied participants into WWP's reports, which the effect doesn't use: 0.8 (0.5-1).

rows.label: Share of the effect that wouldn't have happened anyway, support branch
rows.explainer: Other veteran groups run retreats and peer calls (Team Rubicon, Boulder Crest, the VA's own peer support specialists), and complex cases would often reach VA care later. 0.7 (0.4-0.9).

rows.label: WWP's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: WWP's share of the resources: its share of the cash behind the programmes, with the donated public service announcements that recruit veterans set against all that cash (WWP's full cost over its share), Convention 2.

rows.label: WWP's share of the money behind the programmes
rows.explainer: WWP's grants pay for the Warrior Care Network programmes at no cost to veterans, but the centres bring their own money too: Home Base says it 'operates predominantly on the philanthropic generosity of the Red Sox Foundation, Massachusetts General Hospital and a grateful nation' and received $5M of federal funding for clinical programmes in 2023; the centres' research grants and buildings; some outpatient care billed to TRICARE or VA Community Care; volunteer peer leaders (2,491 volunteers across WWP, 990 Part I line 6). WWP's $35.4M a year is most of the network's programme money at the other three centres. 0.8 (0.4-1).

rows.label: Donated public service announcements allocated to mental health (fair value)

source.title: Wounded Warrior Project, audited consolidated financial statements, year ended 30 September 2025 (Grant Thornton)
source.page: p. 5, statement of functional expenses; note 9

rows.explainer: Airtime donated at the media's rate card, which the auditors allocate to the mental health column; note 9 says PSAs make 'warriors and their families aware of the free programs and services available to them', so they are others' resources behind enrolment.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: WWP's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Delivery adjustment (completion)

source.title: Held et al. (2021), Treatment response trajectories in a three-week CPT-based intensive treatment for veterans with PTSD, Journal of Psychiatric Research 141:226
source.quote: Completion rates for the ITP are high (90.8%)

rows.explainer: Share of those starting who complete: 90.8% at Rush's three-week programme. People who stop early keep part of the gain, so 0.9 (0.8-0.97). Used for the intensive programmes only: the therapy branch's delivery gap is in its dose rows and the support branch's effect is set for the dose delivered.

rows.label: Years a gift waits before it is spent
rows.explainer: WWP held $182.5M of undesignated net assets at 30 September 2025 (audited statement of financial position, p. 3) against $390.3M of yearly spending: about half a year. The board also holds a $219.4M strategic fund and a $103.0M risk reserve (and $191.2M in the Long Term Support Trust), which a new gift may join instead: up to 1.8 years if all net assets count.

rows.label: Discount for the wait before a gift is spent
rows.explainer: The shared discount rate over the wait.

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured: intensive programmes
rows.explainer: Measured: WWP's own count of the veterans who went through the programmes (1,286) meets the trials of the same therapies (CPT and Prolonged Exposure, Kitchiner et al. 2019), and a trial of the daily delivery (Foa et al. 2018) found the massed format as effective. So no missing-data discount (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured: therapy branch
rows.explainer: Thin: the effect is the intensive programmes' scaled by a judged dose, for therapy of unknown content and length.

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured: support branch
rows.explainer: Thin: no controlled evaluation of Project Odyssey, WWP Talk or case coordination; the effect is built from the literature on light-touch support.

rows.label: All adjustments combined, intensive programmes
rows.formula: iop_evidence_adj * iop_counterfactual_adj * attribution_share * implementation_adj * wait_discount * iop_missing_data_adj

rows.label: All adjustments combined, therapy branch
All adjustments combined, support branch
Evidence adjustment (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (iop_wellbys_unadjusted * iop_evidence_adj + opt_wellbys_unadjusted * opt_evidence_adj + sup_wellbys_unadjusted * sup_evidence_adj) / (iop_wellbys_unadjusted + opt_wellbys_unadjusted + sup_wellbys_unadjusted)

rows.label: Counterfactual (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (iop_wellbys_unadjusted * iop_counterfactual_adj + opt_wellbys_unadjusted * opt_counterfactual_adj + sup_wellbys_unadjusted * sup_counterfactual_adj) / (iop_wellbys_unadjusted + opt_wellbys_unadjusted + sup_wellbys_unadjusted)

rows.label: Missing-data step (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (iop_wellbys_unadjusted * iop_missing_data_adj + opt_wellbys_unadjusted * opt_missing_data_adj + sup_wellbys_unadjusted * sup_missing_data_adj) / (iop_wellbys_unadjusted + opt_wellbys_unadjusted + sup_wellbys_unadjusted)

rows.label: All adjustments combined (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: What remains unmodelled, sized: lower substance use and better sleep and return to work after PTSD treatment beyond the depression effect (+0.03: about a quarter of veterans in the intensive programmes have a substance use problem, and gains there partly show up in depression scores already); veterans waiting for a place in an intensive programme instead of starting therapy elsewhere sooner (-0.005: waits are days to weeks). Net 0.025 (-0.03 to 0.08). Co-funders' money is in attribution_share_shared, not here.

rows.label: Yearly suicide rate of US veterans

source.title: US Department of Veterans Affairs (December 2024), VA releases annual Veteran suicide prevention report analyzing 2001-2022 data
source.quote: there were 6,407 suicides among Veterans in 2022

rows.explainer: Per person per year. The VA counted 6,407 veteran suicides in 2022 among about 18 million veterans, about 35 per 100,000, and 46.2 per 100,000 among service members who left in 2021; the veterans treated are mostly 35-55, younger than veterans overall, whose rates are higher. 36 per 100,000 (30-47).

rows.label: Relative risk of suicide with PTSD, against veterans without
rows.explainer: Studies of US veterans find PTSD associated with roughly 1.5 to 2.5 times the suicide rate after adjusting for other psychiatric conditions, much higher unadjusted (Krysinska and Lester 2010, Archives of Suicide Research 14:1, meta-analysis of PTSD and suicide; Conner et al. 2014 and Gradus 2017 in veteran and Danish cohorts). 2 (1.3-4).

rows.label: Share of US veterans with PTSD
rows.explainer: To take the excess out of the all-veteran rate: the National Center for PTSD puts PTSD in a given year at about 5-7% of all veterans and 15-29% of post-9/11 veterans depending on the era; post-9/11 veterans are a fifth of all veterans. 0.12 (0.07-0.2).

rows.label: Yearly suicide rate of veterans without PTSD
rows.explainer: The all-veteran rate with PTSD's excess taken out, so (RR - 1) is applied to the right base.

rows.label: Share of PTSD's excess suicide risk removed at the end of treatment
rows.explainer: Half of Rush's veterans fell below the probable-PTSD cutoff by the end (Held et al. 2021: 50.6%), but losing a diagnosis needn't remove its excess risk, and trials of PTSD therapy have not shown fewer suicides directly. 0.3 (0.1-0.6).

rows.label: Suicides averted per veteran in the intensive programmes (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: The site's recipe (templates.md, wellbeing): the yearly rate × the excess risk × the share removed, over the effect's years as it fades, discounted like the WELLBYs.

rows.label: Suicides averted per person in the therapy branch (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: At the outpatient therapy's dose; counted for the veterans only (opt_veterans), not the family members.

rows.label: Suicides averted per person counselled (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: At counselling's dose, veterans only.

rows.label: Suicides averted per person in the support branch (before adjustments)
rows.formula: deaths_averted_per_person * (sup_effect_sd * sup_effect_duration_years * sup_discount_factor) / (initial_effect_sd * effect_duration_years * discount_factor) * cns_veteran_share
rows.explainer: The same recipe at the support branch's smaller and shorter effect (its SD-years over the intensive programmes'), veterans only (WWP's registrants' share, cns_veteran_share).

rows.label: Share of the deaths averted at ages 15 to 49

source.title: Ptak et al. (2025), Pre-treatment resilience as a predictor of veterans' PTSD symptom outcomes, Journal of Clinical Psychology
source.quote: A total of 727 veterans (age: M = 45.1 years, SD = 10.3) participated in a 2-week Cognitive Processing Therapy (CPT)-based Intensive PTSD Treatment Program

rows.explainer: The veterans' ages: mean 45, SD 10, so about 70% are under 50 (a normal distribution puts 69% below 50); the rest are 50-74.

rows.label: Value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: GiveWell's moral weights for the veterans' age bands, times your value of a life.

rows.label: Deaths averted, in units of value (adjusted)
rows.formula: (people_reached * deaths_averted_per_person * iop_total_adj + (opt_veterans * opt_deaths_per_person + cns_people * cns_deaths_per_person) * opt_total_adj + sup_people * sup_deaths_per_person * sup_total_adj) * value_per_death

rows.label: Deaths averted, in WELLBYs (cancelled by the unit's conversion)
rows.explainer: The one row that puts units of value into WELLBYs; the WELLBY unit's conversion multiplies it back, so the deaths count exactly their shared value at any WELLBY rate.

rows.label: Intensive programmes, WELLBYs before adjustments
